title: Do I Have to Go to Church to Be a Christian?
excerpt: People leave churches because they were hurt, because of hypocrisy and because they were bored, and those reasons are mostly true. No one is saved by attendance. The New Testament still has no picture of a Christian alone by choice, and it speaks differently to the wounded.
body:
A woman stopped going to church the month its leaders took the side of the man who had harmed her, and she has not been inside one in four years. A man in his forties did not leave over anything. The children's games moved to Sunday mornings, a few weeks became a year, and he noticed that he felt about the same. A young father calls himself a Christian, reads the Bible on his phone on the train, listens to sermons while he runs, and has never joined anything.

The skeptic thinks they have all made the sensible choice. The church, he says, is the best argument against Christianity that he knows, and if there is a God a person can surely find him on a hiking trail without the committee meetings.

These are different people and they need different answers, and the first of them comes first. The site has a page for the person who says [the church hurt me](/help/church-hurt), and two of its sentences belong here before any argument. That is a real wound, and you aren't the problem for naming it. If you're safe, you don't have to decide anything about church this week. A crime is a matter for the police whatever a church says about it, and [Find Help](/help) lists where to turn if anyone is still in danger.

## Why People Leave

The reasons people give for leaving are mostly true, and should be granted before anything is said in the church's defense.

Some were hurt. They were shamed or used, or shut out when they told the truth, and the people who did it were quoting the Bible at the time.

Some left over hypocrisy. They watched a congregation preach one thing and protect another. The New Testament would not be surprised. Jesus said of religious leaders that "they tie up heavy burdens, hard to bear, and lay them on people's shoulders, but they themselves are not willing to move them with their finger" (Matthew 23:4). The churches the apostles wrote to were no better behaved than ours. At Corinth there were factions, lawsuits between members, a man living with his father's wife, and a Lord's Supper at which "one goes hungry, another gets drunk" (1 Corinthians 11:21). Paul told them flatly that "when you come together it is not for the better but for the worse" (1 Corinthians 11:17). In the last book of the Bible the risen Christ sends letters to seven congregations and rebukes five of them. Anyone who says the church is full of hypocrites is saying what its own Scriptures said first.

And some were bored. That deserves to be taken seriously too. A great deal of what happens in churches is thin, a weekly program that asks very little and gives about as much, and a person who drifts away from it has not necessarily drifted away from God. The essay on this site about [why people are leaving the church](/writing/the-rise-of-the-nones) follows that story at length.

So the charge is granted. The question is what follows from it.

## What the Question Assumes

The question in the title is a modern sentence, and two of its words would have puzzled the people who wrote the New Testament.

One is "go." In our speech church is a place and an event, something on the calendar that a person attends or skips, like a class. The New Testament's word means an assembly, a people called together. Paul writes "to the church of God that is in Corinth" (1 Corinthians 1:2), and he means the people. They met in houses. Nobody in the first century could have asked whether he had to go to church, any more than a man can ask whether he has to go to his family. He could ask whether he would meet with them.

The other is "have to." It treats the church as a requirement to be met, a fee for membership in something else. The question quietly assumes that being a Christian is a private arrangement between one person and God, with the congregation as an optional supplement. That assumption feels natural to us because we absorbed it long before we read a Bible. The essay here on [how American individualism distorts the Bible](/writing/how-american-individualism-distorts) traces where it came from. It did not come from the apostles.

## What the New Testament Says

The plain answer to the question as asked has to be given first, because the gospel is at stake in it. No one is made right with God by attendance. "By grace you have been saved through faith. And this is not your own doing; it is the gift of God, not a result of works" (Ephesians 2:8-9). A man crucified beside Jesus was promised paradise that afternoon without having sat through a single service. If the question is whether churchgoing saves a person, the answer is no, and any church that says otherwise has confused itself with its Lord.

But the New Testament has no picture of a Christian who lives the faith alone by preference. On the first day anyone preached the resurrection, "those who received his word were baptized, and there were added that day about three thousand souls. And they devoted themselves to the apostles' teaching and the fellowship, to the breaking of bread and the prayers" (Acts 2:41-42). Believing and being added are told as one event.

The letters assume it everywhere. Nearly all of them are addressed to congregations. Their commands are written in the plural and most of them can't be carried out alone: "Bear one another's burdens" (Galatians 6:2), "confess your sins to one another and pray for one another" (James 5:16). Baptism is something no one can do to himself, and the Supper is a shared meal by definition. Paul's chief picture of the church is a body, and he draws the inference himself: "The eye cannot say to the hand, 'I have no need of you'" (1 Corinthians 12:21). An eye by itself has stopped being of any use as an eye.

One passage speaks to the matter directly. It was written to believers under real pressure, some of whom had begun to stay away, and it does not scold them. It gives them a reason: "let us consider how to stir up one another to love and good works, not neglecting to meet together, as is the habit of some, but encouraging one another" (Hebrews 10:24-25). The meeting is for the sake of the others in the room. A person who is absent is also withholding something.

Scripture does know believers who were alone. An Ethiopian official was baptized on a desert road and "went on his way rejoicing" (Acts 8:39), back to a country where, so far as the text tells us, there was no one to meet with. John was "on the island called Patmos" (Revelation 1:9), sent there for his preaching, and the Lord's day found him there. The Bible does not treat isolation by circumstance as a failure. Solitude as a preference is the thing it never describes.

## The Trail

The skeptic's trail deserves an answer of its own, because he is partly right. Scripture says that "the heavens declare the glory of God" (Psalm 19:1), and solitude belongs to the Christian life. Luke says of Jesus that "he would withdraw to desolate places and pray" (Luke 5:16). Once he spent a whole night alone on a mountain. Luke also records what he did when day came: he called his disciples and chose twelve of them (Luke 6:12-13).

What a trail can't do is tell a person anything he had not already thought. Nobody on it will contradict him or ask anything of him. The Christian message is news about something that happened, and news has to be brought by someone. "How are they to hear without someone preaching?" Paul asks (Romans 10:14). Left to ourselves we arrive, sooner or later, at a God who agrees with us.

## How Christians Have Said It

One of the earliest descriptions of a Christian Sunday outside the New Testament was written around the year 150 by Justin, a Christian teacher in Rome. "All who live in cities or in the country gather together to one place," he told the emperor, and he went on to list what they did there: the reading of the apostles and prophets, a sermon, prayers, bread and wine, and a collection for orphans, widows, the sick and prisoners. Deacons carried a portion of the bread to those who were absent.

That last detail answers a question that is asked more often now, when a service can be watched from a kitchen. For someone who is ill, or housebound, or far from any congregation, a broadcast is a mercy. The second-century church had its own provision for such people. When a member could not come to the gathering, someone was sent to bring the gathering to him. Christians who can come and choose the screen for its convenience are in a different position from the people those deacons visited.

A century later Cyprian, bishop of Carthage, put the claim in its strongest form: "He can no longer have God for his Father, who has not the Church for his mother." The Catholic and Orthodox churches have kept that conviction in its strong form: the church is where Christ has promised to give himself, and she is not optional.

The Reformers kept more of it than their heirs often realize. The Westminster Confession calls the visible church "the house and family of God, out of which there is no ordinary possibility of salvation." The word "ordinary" is chosen with care. It leaves room for the thief on the cross and the believer in a prison cell, and it refuses to make them the model. The Reformers also gave a test for what counts. The Lutheran confession of 1530 defines the church as "the congregation of saints, in which the Gospel is rightly taught and the Sacraments are rightly administered." By that test a body that preaches something other than the gospel, or uses its power to devour its members, is failing to be a church, and leaving it is no departure from one.

The experiment of solitary faith has been tried by serious people. In the fourth century many went into the Egyptian desert to seek God alone, and the history course on this site tells what they found. Solitude damaged a good number of them, and before long the hermits were being gathered into communities with a common table and a rule. Basil of Caesarea, who carried that way of life into the Greek-speaking church, is remembered there for his question to the monk who flees everyone: whose feet will he wash?

## Why It Was Never Meant to Be Done Alone

Basil's question goes to the root. Nearly everything Jesus commands needs another person. A man can't forgive in an empty room, or be patient there, or take the lower seat. "By this all people will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another" (John 13:35). John is blunter: "he who does not love his brother whom he has seen cannot love God whom he has not seen" (1 John 4:20).

A faith practiced alone is a faith in which no one ever irritates us, contradicts us, needs a ride at an inconvenient hour, or sings the songs we dislike. That is its appeal, and the appeal is the trouble with it. We have learned to choose a church the way we choose anything else, by what it offers us, and to leave when it stops offering it. The complaint that church is boring is often fair. It also takes for granted that the gathering exists for the person attending. Hebrews has it the other way around.

Those of us who stayed have little to be proud of here. We built churches that were easy to leave, because they asked for nothing and knew no one by name. We made the service a performance and then blamed the audience for walking out. And when people left, we found it simpler to call them lazy or bitter than to ask what they had seen.

## If the Church Is Where You Were Hurt

Everything above applies differently to someone the church has harmed, and it should be said plainly.

The same help page answers the question whether it is all right to leave, and its answer is worth having whole: If a church is abusive, leaving can be the faithful choice, and leaving a congregation isn't leaving Christ. The Bible is not on the side of the institution here. Through Ezekiel, God speaks about leaders who fed on the people in their care: "Behold, I am against the shepherds, and I will require my sheep at their hand" (Ezekiel 34:10). Then he says what he will do instead: "I myself will search for my sheep and will seek them out" (Ezekiel 34:11). The one who goes looking in that passage is God, and he is looking for the sheep that were driven off.

So no one may use Hebrews 10 as a stick on a person who is staying away from the place where she was wounded. That verse was written to encourage frightened people, and it gives no one the right to herd them. The help page says that the way back, when there is one, can begin very small, with one or two Christians who are trusted. Jesus set the minimum lower than any church does: "where two or three are gathered in my name, there am I among them" (Matthew 18:20). The essay on [doubt after abuse by a church leader](/writing/doubt-after-church-abuse) was written for this, and [Find Help](/help) is there for anything more urgent.

## What Remains

The young father with the Bible on his phone isn't a hypocrite, and nobody needs to tell him his faith is false. What the New Testament would ask him is practical. Who knows him well enough to tell him when he is wrong? Whose burden is he carrying, and who is carrying his? Who will stand with him at his father's grave? A podcast will do none of it.

Much of what a congregation is for happens on days when nothing is scheduled. Someone notices that a widow's car hasn't moved, and someone drives a neighbor to chemotherapy. A man tells an older man the thing he has told no one, and is prayed for by name. Paul's instruction is short: "Rejoice with those who rejoice, weep with those who weep" (Romans 12:15). It can't be done for people one has never met.

The man who drifted is asked something similar, without any reproach. He feels about the same as he did, and he may be right about that. The New Testament's interest is in whether anyone else has been poorer for his being gone.

For the woman, the question can wait as long as it needs to. The door she walked out of may be one she should never go back through. Scripture describes the church as a body, and also as a bride: "Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her" (Ephesians 5:25). He knows better than anyone what has been done in her name, and he has not said he is finished with her. That is a hard thing to hear for someone the church has injured, and it is not offered here as a reason to return. It is only the reason the question does not finally go away.

*"The eye cannot say to the hand, 'I have no need of you.'"* (1 Corinthians 12:21)

*"Behold, I, I myself will search for my sheep and will seek them out."* (Ezekiel 34:11)
